excerpt: Search for products with text, image, or URL
Layer on filters like price, brand, category, dimensions, and attributes
Structured product data, with a consistent schema across retailers
When your users make a purchase, Channel3 records the sale and pays you a percentage of the sale price.
Access 100 million+ products from 25,000+ brands through one API.
Pass any product URL and get structured metadata: pricing, variants, images, and merchant offers in a single response.
Scraping is fragile and expensive... Channel3 provides one normalized, structured product graph
Image search — Turn any photo or screenshot into product results across 100M+ items.
You can use it without writing any code, and without an API key.
If your agent already supports UCP, connect it to Channel3's global catalog for product search and lookup across stores.
Connect Cursor, VS Code, Claude, ChatGPT, Codex, or OpenCode.
Install the Channel3 SDK, authenticate, and make async calls.
The Channel3 CLI calls the Channel3 API from a terminal or script.
Search from a public image URL or local image file.
Select formats or extract fields with JMESPath.
When you subscribe to price tracking for a product, you can receive webhook notifications whenever the price changes.
You get 1000 free credits every month, and extra credits are billed as they're used, at just $0.007 each.
No account? Agents can pay via MPP (Machine Payments Protocol) — no API key or signup required.
Optional user identifier to attribute clicks and sales to a user in your system. Channel3 appends it to buy URLs in the response.
Toggle to agentic mode, and an LLM plans the search: it extracts deterministic filters, may split the request into OR/AND sub-searches
Pasted identifiers — SKU, MPN, GTIN, UPC, or EAN that should pin and boost an exact match
No OAuth flow is required for the public product data API. API keys are free to create.

Searching "nintendo switch 2" gave sketchy results. The first had "hong kong" in the title even though the product is said to be US-only, and the store was "My Nintendo Store PT" (Portuguese). The second result was a dress, unrelated to video games.

User saw irrelevant results for many queries. For "plain white pillowcase", the 3rd result was a t-shirt, the 7th a dress and the 11th a light bulb. For "men's wallet", the very first result was an outdoor picnic table.
Searching for Ryzen 9950X3D returned 6 different AMD processors, then a fully built PC containing that chip. The actual product the user wanted was ranked 16th.

Searching "red high top sneakers under $40" returned a shaft seal first. The next result was a correct sneaker but showed a price of '0'. After that came basically random items (skin care, dog food, white sneakers, dog bandanas), and the price limit started being ignored.

"Seems like a great idea but the search is horrible." Products were completely unrelated, or matched only on a keyword. The user warned that releasing too early may hurt, since most people won't retry if quality is bad.
"Great idea but the search is awful which is dissapointing given how mainstream search has gotten."
Searches for "dog collar" and "cat scratching post" were not confidence-inspiring: missing prices, blurry or weird photos.
A developer building a product on top of Channel3 says the team is very responsive and the product is getting better every day.

User sees affiliate revenue flowing through Channel3 as the key selling point. Their past attempts at direct affiliate sign-ups failed: complicated forms across networks, months-long waits, and rejection for a small non-review site (including by Amazon). They may revive their site using Channel3.
"$7 per 1000 searches seems steep." The user won't sign up without knowing whether they'll make money, given they'd also share commission with Channel3.
User would try the product only if the 1,000 free-search limit were raised, arguing it should be opened up since Channel3 already takes a revenue share.
Criticism of the "every product on the Internet" claim versus the product being US-only: "Is it even 1 % of all products on the Internet?"
User noted that product country-of-origin info isn't shown.
User was confused about who the product is for: end buyers searching an aggregator, or developers building their own e-commerce search. They found the positioning unclear.
User questioned the differentiation, showing that simply prompting a foundation model (e.g. "show me outdoor grills, between 500 and 1000, from weber") already produces comparable product results.
